It is also an economic question, and for the countries most exposed, a development question too. More than 80% of world merchandise trade by volume moves by sea. When a choke point is disrupted, the shock travels quickly through freight and insurance costs, energy and food prices, supply chains and household budgets, foreign currencies and debt markets. Recent events show how quickly this happens. In the Straits of Hormuz, tanker freight has risen to record levels. As of late August, certain rates between the Middle East and East Asia have climbed above $120 per ton, which is triple the rate a year ago. War risk premiums remain elevated. Few ship owners are willing to enter. Since July, these pressures are now being compounded by a second choke point. Renewed disruptions around Bab el-Mandeb have affected a route that had itself become an alternative to Hormuz. For Saudi crude, ships from Jambol to South Korea, avoiding Bab el-Mandeb extends delivery from about 24 days to roughly 54 days, which is one additional month at sea. The result is more fuel consumed, more vessel capacity tied up in transit, higher costs, and higher emissions. Port congestion is magnifying the pressure. The stakes extend directly to food security. Around one third of global seaborn fertilizer trade which is about 16 million tons, normally passes through Hormuz. Natural gas is also a key input for nitrogen-based fertilizers. When energy, fertilizer, and transport costs rise together, they affect planting decisions, yields, food prices, and of course, future harvests. And the burden is not shared equally. Many are least developed countries, small island developing states, or economies already facing high debt service burdens and limited fiscal space. Landlocked developing countries may be far from the sea, but their exposure runs through a limited number of transit corridors and neighboring ports. Mr. Chairman, Excellencies, distinguished members of the Security Council, fellow briefers. They are civilians. They are not parties to geopolitical conflicts. As such, they must not be become collateral to those, Mr. Chairman. The situation in the Strait of Hormuz and the region demonstrates why this matters. The human cost is devastating. 22 seafarers have already sadly lost their lives, not to mention the many more such casualties at the Black Sea and elsewhere. These are not statistics. They are people who went to sea to do their job and support their families. This is not simply a shipping crisis. It is a crisis for people, for trade, and for the global economy. In addition to this very serious humanitarian issue, we also raised today our major concern regarding the legal status of the strait. RCS position is clear. The Strait of Hormuz is a maritime passage used for international navigation, and the right of transit passage must be respected in accordance with international law. The ability of commercial ships to navigate international waters safely, predictably, and without unnecessary impediment is crucial to international maritime law and to the global trade system. Straits, therefore, cannot become a place where commercial shipping is required to obtain permission, negotiate its passage, or accept arbitrary restrictions simply because geopolitical tensions have escalated. This is not a privilege to be granted or withdrawn according to political circumstances of the day. It is a fundamental legal principle of this very house and organization. And if that principle is weakened in one international strait, the consequences will not stop at the Strait of Hormuz, the Red Sea, or the Strait of Bab al-Mandab, but will extend far beyond the region and far beyond shipping. Ultimately, It will disproportionately affect developing countries, small island states, and countries that heavily depend on imported energy and food. Excellencies, we are already seeing the consequences when shipping is forced away from established routes. Rerouting adds days or weeks to voyages, consumes additional fuel, requires additional ships and crew time, and increases emissions. Excellencies, For these reasons, there must not be compulsory tolls or transit charges for lawful passage through any international strait, including Hormuz. As we have written to the UN Security Council President earlier in August, the United Nations and governments must not allow a toll to be called a service fee, a coordination charge, a clearance payment, or something else, and thereby create the same result. A strategic international waterway must not become a political tollgate. Otherwise, the political message from such action, or better still, inaction, will be equally clear. Mr. President, Excellencies, Distinguished members of the Security Council, Thank you for the opportunity to draw attention to a group of workers who are too often invisible, in particular when conflict affects international shipping: the seafarers on board. For them, The ongoing maritime security crisis is not an abstract disruption to global trade. It is a direct threat to their lives. According to the International Maritime Organization, since the current conflict in the Middle East began on 28 February, 80 attacks on merchant vessels have been verified in and around the Strait of Hormuz. At least 22 seafarers have lost their lives and many others have been injured, as we have also just heard. In April this year, the officers of the special tripartite committee of the Maritime Labour Convention, that includes the International Chamber of Shipping and the International Transport Federation, have expressed their grave concern about approximately 20,000 seafarers stranded in that area. They called for urgent cooperation to safeguard their lives, safety and well-being. Five months later, thousands of seafarers remain affected by the disruption. Around 5,000 have not been able to leave their vessels and are still stranded in those waters. Thousands continue sailing through waters threatened by missiles, drones and mines with a real fear that each day could be their last. Numerous seafarers find themselves in situations of abandonment, without wages, food, water or electricity. Many are unable to go ashore, receive medical treatment, be replaced by colleagues, or return home. Communication with family and friends is often very difficult. Excellencies, our message today is simple. Conflicts do not suspend seafarers' fundamental rights. The ILO Maritime Labour Convention, adopted in 2006, continues to apply in times of crisis. And it is precisely during these periods that the protection it provides should be more scrupulously enforced. This convention, ratified by 113 member states representing more than 96% of the world fleet, guarantees seafarers' fundamental right to a healthy and safe environment. It provides protections concerning the quality of food and water, repatriation, health and medical care on board, and, more broadly, the right to decent working and living conditions. In particular, seafarers requiring immediate medical care must be given access to medical facilities ashore. In 2025, the Convention was amended, building on a UN General Assembly resolution, to formally recognize seafarers as key workers and to request Member States to protect their rights at all times, including the rights to shore leave, medical care and repatriation. The reality today shows that rights on paper are not enough for seafarers who are trapped aboard vessels in conflict zones. There is another fundamental issue. In April, the officers of the Special Tripartite Committee also emphasized that seafarers must be able to freely choose whether to work in high-risk areas without fear of negative consequences for their future employment. According to the information available to the International Labour Organization, that principle is not a reality for all seafarers. We therefore need stronger arrangements in place to support seafarers during this and future crises. Ladies and gentlemen, let me highlight two practical measures. First, India has recently proposed the establishment of an international emergency support network for seafarers, linking maritime authorities and diplomatic missions to provide seafarers with rapid assistance during emergencies. This proposal deserves careful consideration. The ILO has been working closely with the IMO and the international social partners to address the situation of affected seafarers, in particular those in need of urgent assistance. However, more needs to be done. Second, we must ensure the full and effective implementation of the protections that already exist in the Maritime Labour Convention and other important UN and IMO treaties. In the medium term, the ILO Office stands ready to support tripartite discussions on any proposals for amendments to the MLC that could further reinforce existing protections and strengthen our collective capacity to respond when normal arrangements break down. Excellencies, seafarers keep global supply chains moving. during pandemics and periods of extraordinary danger at sea. They should never be considered collateral damage of maritime insecurity. The international community has established the standards. Our urgent responsibility now is to ensure that those standards translate into protection, assistance, and safe passage for every seafarer. Thank you.

Today, we face a significant erosion of the rules and norms that have long governed the sea, and it is time for the Security Council and the international community not only to react, but to anticipate, to steer us back into safer waters and work towards global maritime peace. The age of gray zone strategy and tactics has arrived at sea, and that implies that many of our categories of what counts as responsible conduct are eroding, and the challenges are mounting on every front. We see a growing number of kinetic attacks on merchant ships by states and non-state actors. In the Western Indian Ocean, a dramatic resurgence of piracy is reversing decades of hard-won success. Uncertainty is growing across the globe over how strategic waterways, the canals and straits that we all depend on, should be governed and how safety should be organized. New ambiguities have arisen over who has the right to enforce what kind of sanctions and over when boarding and seizures of civilian vessels are legitimate. We lack clear rules for the responsible use of naval mines and drones. but also for digital interference, including spoofing and jamming of signals. On top of that, blue crimes, whether that's smuggling, deliberate pollution, or illicit fishing, remain rampant worldwide, and as a result, marine biodiversity is in decline. Many of the regional maritime security architectures that we have built over decades are too weak to cope with any of this. Maritime security is a global responsibility. It requires the whole UN system to work concertedly. For that, we need to look beyond the current Strait of Formosa situation and recognize that we are not facing a set of localized emergencies. It is a larger crisis of the maritime order itself. And this really needs to sink in and it needs strategic consequences. Above all, we need a process to organize the global dialogue on responsible behavior at sea. Those of us in the research community, including at UNITAR, have long pointed out that maritime security has no natural home in the UN system. We lack the systematic information and analysis that is needed to inform strategic choices. Many UN agencies, some of which we have heard from today, are active in this domain, but there is no sustainable strategy and too little ambition to coordinate. Fixing that problem would also make the UN's work more effective and less costly, would save money. The Security Council is vital not only as a place for dialogue, but also for advancing the sustainable strategy for maritime security. I would like to reiterate that many of the options of how to proceed in the Council and beyond are already on the table. Let me emphasize three concrete steps here. First, At a very minimum, make maritime security a standing issue on the Council's agenda, an annual debate ideally informed by an annual state of maritime security report from the Secretary General. Second, think further. Appoint a special envoy or convene a blue ribbon panel to develop stronger options for dialogue and addressing the knowledge gaps and norm deficits. Third, and perhaps most consequential in the long run, work towards establishing a permanent clearinghouse mechanism, a center of competence, a center of excellence that can provide the data that is needed, the expertise, the legal analysis, the coordination function that the domain currently lacks. The clock is ticking in many ways. People are suffering now and they will do so in the future if no strategic vision is developed and concrete steps are actually being taken. And there's no less at stake than the global order and global maritime peace. Thank you so much.

This state of play has now rapidly shifted as increasingly ruthless state actors attempt to use international waterways as leverage to essentially blackmail the world by threatening critical supply chains and global economy. Maritime security and the well-established norms of freedom of navigation have therefore become a major challenge on the global stage. This issue has never been as prominent for maintenance of peace and security and for the Security Council agenda as it is now, so this discussion could not be timelier. Iran and Russia have been disrupting global maritime commerce for their own political gain in complete disregard of international law and the humanitarian economic consequences of their actions. These attacks have escalated recently, killing and injuring seafarers of various nations, targeting civilian vessels, merchant vessels, even flagged and owned by third countries. Crucially, these targeted vessels are transporting grain to supply countries across the globe, desperately needed for the world's poorest. These actions share an immoral strategy of trying to gain geopolitical advantage and putting pressure on one's opponents at the expense of vulnerable populations in other parts of the world. Worryingly, we are seeing a similar pattern reemerging in the Red Sea and around the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, as this critical global waterway is increasingly under the threat of intimidation and attack from the Iran-backed Houthis. To be clear, all economies across the globe are affected by attacks and threats on freedom of navigation. be it in Hormuz, the Red Sea or Black Sea. Among these threats, we must include the shadow fleets, operating outside any safety parameters to unlawfully evade sanctions. And another key risk stems from sabotaging the subsea cable infrastructure worldwide. Finally, a robust and meaningful response to these complex challenges involves a multilayered effort. First, we must redouble on our commitment and strengthen the implementation of international law at sea, as reflected in the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea. International waterways are governed by clear legal principles and no political considerations may interfere with freedom of navigation. Another layer is increased awareness raising and coordination at all levels, most notably within the IMO, but also in regional organizations and other fora, while keeping the Security Council seized on threats that undermine navigational rights and freedoms. mechanisms such as US-led initiatives and the proposed UK-France-led defensive mission for the Strait of Hormuz.

Also have a practical role to play. To address marine supply chain disruptions and sabotage.

States must work collectively with the private sector to establish redundancies, determine alternatives, and identify gaps before the next crisis arrives. while implementing international sanctions and closely cooperating with the flag states to combat the use of unsafe vessels. To conclude, Excellency, allow me to conclude by reiterating our call for an immediate cessation of attacks against lawful civilian shipping, including in and around the Strait of Hormuz, the Red Sea, and against the Ukrainian grain export infrastructure in the Black Sea. Latvia will remain a steadfast defender of maritime security and free and safe navigation.

Thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Latvia for her statement, and I will give the floor to the distinguished representative of Liberia. You have the floor, sir.

Thank you, Your Excellency. We join in expressing our gratitude to the delegation of Bahrain for convening us and joining, welcoming you, Your Excellency, to this meeting and thank certainly the briefers for their insightful comments. The point bears emphasizing. When a single maritime choke point closes, it is not just ships that are stranded. It is the lifeline of the global economy that gets blocked. As the world's largest ship registry by gross tonnage, Liberia speaks from the front line of commercial navigation. When a missile strikes the Red Sea or a mine threatens the Strait of Hormuz, the shock waves do not stop at the water's edge. They reverberate directly into consumer markets, driving up freight and insurance premiums, and turning daily bread, energy, and fertilizer into unaffordable luxuries for millions across the global south, most acutely across Africa. The briefers are right. Navigation of freedom is not an abstract concept. It is the circulatory system of human survival. To preserve it, Liberia presents three imperatives. First, law must govern the waves. Freedom of navigation and transit passage are not privileges granted at political discretion. They are universal rights codified in UNCLOS and the U.N. Charter. The international community must never normalize unilateral interference, harassment, or lawlessness across critical international waterways. Second, we must replace escalation with neutral multilateral deconfliction. Military buildup alone cannot guarantee commercial passage. Liberia backs the Secretary-General's good offices to establish a neutral UN-led deconfliction framework focused on insulating civilian merchant vessels and safeguarding critical flows of grain and fertilizer. To endure, this architecture must remain technical, rules-based and anchored in close cooperation with regional littoral states and the International Maritime Organization. Third, civilian seafarers must never be collateral damage. Merchant mariners are noncombatants. They are the quiet backbone of international trade. It is unconscionable that those who feed and power our world face captive detention, physical peril, and targeted attacks. Liberia demands rapid rescue and repatriation protocols, unimpeded medical access, and zero impunity for assaults on commercial crews. Excellencies, Our duty in this council is unambiguous. We must secure our oceans for the benefit of humanity, not militarize it for confrontation. Firmly aligned with the African Union's maritime vision, Liberia stands ready to bridge divides and protect our common arteries. The seas belong to shared human progress. Let us defend them together and keep it that way. I thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Liberia for his statement. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of the United Kingdom. You have the floor.

Thank you, Excellency. The United Kingdom thanks the Kingdom of Bahrain for her leadership in bringing this important matter to the Council. We welcome the focus of this meeting on safeguarding freedom of navigation and strengthening the resilience of critical maritime routes. Thank you to the briefers for their expert contributions. As a maritime nation, the United Kingdom has a long-standing commitment to maritime security. and to defending the rules-based international order at sea. We are resolute in upholding the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea, which sets the legal framework for all activities in the oceans and seas. Over the last five years, the world has experienced major maritime disruptions in the Black Sea, the Red Sea, the Strait of Hormuz, and this trend risks continuing if we don't act now and together. The Houthis' decision to resume conflict in Yemen, their continued strikes in the region and on Saudi Arabia, and their reckless attacks in the Red Sea threaten freedom of navigation, transit passage, and undermine maritime security in the Bab al-Mandab. Actions by Russia, Iran, and their proxies have significantly eroded international security, cost the lives of seafarers, burdened the global economy indiscriminately, often hitting the world's most vulnerable people. Wheat prices rose 25% between January and July this year. Prolonged disruption across vital routes will only add further pressure to global food security and disrupt access at fertiliser and food. The impact on cost of living is immediate and it is global. Navigational rights and freedoms, including the right of transit passage through international straits, must be upheld and protected. Commercial shipping and seafarers' lives must not be used as leverage. Unlawful restrictions or tolls must not be imposed on international waterways. The stability of the network of sea lanes covering the worldwide maritime domain is a global common good from which we all benefit. Disruption in any part of this network can rapidly generate economic and security impacts well beyond the immediate region. Maritime security is too often treated as a regional issue, when a concerted international effort will be needed to protect the whole of this vital and globally connected domain. And we urge all states to speak out against unlawful maritime disruption. The security of our critical maritime routes is a shared responsibility. The United Kingdom remains committed to working with Bahrain, with the International Maritime Organization, and with partners across the international community to uphold international law, to defend freedom of navigation, to protect seafarers, and to strengthen the resilience of the maritime routes on which our world depends. Thank you, Excellency.
I thank the distinguished representative of the United Kingdom for her statement, and I'll give the floor to the distinguished representative of China. You have the floor.

Chair, I welcome His Excellency Minister of Foreign Affairs, Al Zayani, for presiding over this meeting, and I thank all the briefers for their presentations. The ocean serves as a vital link connecting countries, while international shipping links are the arteries of the global economy. Recently, navigation through the Strait of Hormuz has been disrupted, while risks to maritime security in the Bab el-Mandab Strait and the Red Sea have increased. These developments have affected global energy and food security as well as the stability of industrial and supply chains, with particularly pronounced impacts on the Global South. All parties should uphold the spirit of cooperation and properly address the risks and challenges. I would like to make four points. First, work towards an immediate ceasefire and an end to the hostilities. Fundamentally, disruptions to international shipping links are the spillover effects of the conflict. Unless the fighting on land is brought to an end, it will be difficult to fully restore security at sea. All parties concerned, particularly Israel, should sincerely and fully implement the ceasefire agreement and work towards achieving genuine and lasting peace in Gaza. We encourage the US and Iran to maintain rational and exercise restraint, return to the Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding as soon as possible, and on the basis of consensus reached thus far, reconstruct the negotiation mechanisms and engage in substantive consultations on issues of concerns to both sides. China does not wish to see regional tensions further spill over into Yemen and the Red Sea, and calls on all parties to stop further complicating the situation. and to resolve issues through dialogue and consultations. Second, uphold the basic principles of international law. The UN Charter and international law must remain the fundamental norms governing the handling of Middle East affairs. The international community, in particular major powers from outside the region, should reject double standards, respect the sovereignty and territorial integrity of countries in the region, and refrain from readily resorting to the use of force or unilateral sanctions. Humanitarian issues must not be politicized. All parties to the conflicts are obligated to strictly abide by international humanitarian law, ensure safe and unimpeded access for humanitarian assistance, and avoid attacks on civilians and civilian infrastructure. Third, help alleviate the difficulties facing countries of the Global South. The rights of commercial vessels of all countries to navigate in accordance with international law should be respected by all parties. China urges all parties to take effective measures to reopen the Strait of Hormuz at an early date and safeguard the safety and unimpeded flow of international shipping links. China supports dialogue between the Gulf countries and Iran based on mutual respect for territorial sovereignty and national security, and to safeguard the common interests of the region in a constructive manner. China welcomes Secretary-General Guterres' initiative to establish an operational mechanism for the Strait of Hormuz and supports a greater role for the UN. Fourth, promote the building of a new security architecture for the Middle East. The current situation once again demonstrates that the existing security architecture in the region is inadequate and needs to be reformed and strengthened. We call for the people of the Middle East to determine their own future and support countries in the region in strengthening dialogue on peace and security and exploring ways to reshape the regional security architecture. Efforts should be made to seek comprehensive solutions to hotspot issues and advance a more integrated approach to common security in the region. China supports countries in the region in embracing a vision of common, comprehensive, cooperative, and sustainable security, developing good neighborly and friendly relations, and achieving peaceful coexistence. Chair, the disruption of international shipping links reflects deep-seated problems in global security governance. Recently, President Xi Jinping has put forward four proposals for maintaining and promoting peace and stability in the Middle East. four principles for advancing the solution of the Palestinian issue, and four initiatives for building common security in the Middle East, thereby contributing China's solution to achieving long-term stability and peace in the region as a whole. China has always stood on the side of peace, on the side of dialogue, and on the right side of history, and will, as always, contribute to promoting reconciliation and negotiations, upholding fairness and justice, and maintaining peace and stability. I thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of China for her statement. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Denmark. You have the floor, madam.

Your Excellency, Minister Al-Sayani, we thank you for your presence, and we thank Bahrain for hosting today's ARIA meeting. I also would like to thank all the briefers for their important contributions today. Chair, as a top 10 global shipping nation, Denmark is acutely aware of the importance of maritime security. The world's oldest long-distance mode of transport remains the backbone of the global economy, moving around 85% of international trade. It is one of the key factors underpinning the interconnected world. Open sea lanes are vital to international peace and security. This is particularly the case for food and energy security. Attacks in recent years on commercial ships in the Black Sea, the Red Sea, in the Strait of Hormuz and the Gulf of Oman have caused spikes in energy and commodity prices.

As always, this has impacted the most vulnerable across the world.

Tragically, increased food insecurity is now a certainty for millions. with less grain available for immediate consumption and less fertilizers for crops in the next growing season. The recent instability in the Bab al-Mandeb Strait only exacerbates these pressures. It is a very concerning development. Throughout Denmark's term on the Security Council, we have consistently focused on food security, including in our August signature event on conflict and hunger. Such debates have shown how critical waterways impact food security, most notably in the Global South. Chair, Denmark's approach to maritime security is anchored in the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea. In international straits, unencumbered passage must be the starting point. We cannot permit littoral states to threaten or attack commercial shipping. We unequivocally condemn the illegal obstruction of key international straits. We also recall the thousands of seafarers trapped on vessels or in ports in the Gulf.

As we have heard about from Madame Adrees today.

We demand that they be allowed to return to their loved ones in safety. Iran's de facto closure of the Strait of Hormuz is unacceptable and it's unlawful. Denmark is ready to participate in the UK-French-led, independent and strictly defensive multinational military mission in support of freedom of navigation in the Strait of Hormuz, once conditions allow. Denmark also contributes to the EU maritime operation ESDP in the Red Sea to defend freedom of navigation. Chair, in closing, maritime security is a prerequisite for global peace, stability and prosperity. UNCLOS and the freedom of navigation must be upheld. Denmark will continue to work with partners to keep maritime routes open, to safeguard the flow of food and energy, and ensure no country can use critical waterways as instruments of coercion. We believe the Security Council has a vital role to play in this. I thank you.

I thank the distinguished.

Representative of Denmark for her statements. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Pakistan. You have the floor, sir.

Excellency, Foreign Minister, we are pleased to see you preside over this important meeting organized by the Kingdom of Bahrain. And I would like to join colleagues in thanking our briefers for sharing their valuable insights. President, the concept of maritime security has evolved over time and one of the major achievements of post-World War II order is open, safe and free maritime space, which ushered in a rapid development of global economy, trade and investment. The global maritime domain is presently in the grip of intractable challenges. It has morphed into a locus of intensifying global geopolitical competition and the intersecting challenges of the 21st century. Myriad nontraditional threats ranging from piracy and terrorism to human trafficking and climate-induced risks have added another layer of complexity to this existing challenge. Disruption of commercial shipping and attacks on merchant vessels, both in the Strait of Hormuz and Bab al-Mandab, has underscored that crises at sea have grave implications for continents and countries. The volatility at these maritime chokes have not only imperiled peace and stability, but also skyrocketed energy prices and heightened fears of global food insecurity. The Strait of Hormuz is a critical maritime trade route for the transit of one-third of globally traded crude oil and a significant share of global fertilizer trade. Its geostrategic location also makes it vital for region security and stability. Pakistan is deeply concerned at the disruptions in the Strait, including attacks on commercial shipping. We reiterate our strong support for the sovereignty and territorial integrity of our brotherly countries in the region which are adversely impacted by the volatility and violence in the Strait. Pakistan calls for an immediate de-escalation of tensions, security of ships and crew members navigating through the Strait, and restoration of normal passage through the Strait. Pakistan strongly condemns the nefarious designs of Houthi militia to weaponize Bab al-Mandab by launching attacks on merchant shipping and innocent seafarers navigating the Strait. These attacks seriously undermine maritime security and threaten peace and development of regional countries, especially the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, which is facing blatant and unprovoked aggression by the Houthis. Pakistan reaffirms its unwavering support for the sovereignty, territorial integrity, security and prosperity of the Kingdom and stands in complete solidarity with its leadership, government and brothers and sisters. We call upon Houthi militia for immediate cessation of these provocative acts which could have dire consequences for maritime security and regional peace and stability. President, as one of the literal states of Indian Ocean with overwhelming reliance on sea-borne trade and as a party to UN Convention on Law of the Sea, Pakistan attaches paramount importance to maritime safety and security. It is our principal position that global shipping should not become a casualty of conflict and strife. Instead, it should remain a driver of global trade and economy. Guided by these foundational principles, Pakistan acted as a mediator between Iran and the United States following the outbreak of hostilities between the two countries. With the support of our friends and partners, we spearheaded diplomatic efforts for de-escalation and broader regional stability, culminating in a ceasefire and Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding. We shall continue to make efforts for a negotiated settlement of all outstanding issues for an early return to normalcy at sea and land. In pursuit of this objective, Pakistan looks forward to working with all peace-loving nations in region and beyond for furtherance of maritime peace and security and safety of commercial shipping and merchant vessels. I thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Pakistan for the statement. I give the floor now to the distinguished representative of Panama. You have the floor.

Thank you very much, Chair. As a maritime nation, the Republic of Panama welcomes and recognizes the initiative of the Kingdom of Bahrain, as well as your sustained efforts to promote maritime security and to highlight its contribution to international peace and security. And we'd also like to cordially welcome His Excellency, Mr. Abdul Latif bin Rashid Al Zayani, Minister of Foreign Affairs of the Kingdom of Bahrain. This initiative is particularly relevant, given the growing vulnerability of the major shipping routes over recent months. Critical maritime corridors such as the Hormuz Straits and most recently the Bab al-Mandab straits in the Red Sea have been affected by situations contrary to international law that have interrupted or hindered free transit, leading to disruptions in global trade and endangering supply chains, particularly those related to the energy sector. These events demonstrate, I think, the challenges facing the international community in guaranteeing respect for international law and the effective implementation of Security Council resolutions. We cannot allow these actions to normalize lack of respect for international law or reduce our collective ability to respond effectively to these situations. Chair, in this context, we are very concerned as we see the recent reports about the growing use of AI tools by the Houthis to strengthen their military capacities, including the development of guided missile systems to attack vessels. in a situation where we have seen repeated attacks against commercial vessels in the Red Sea and elsewhere. This shows how technologies that are increasingly accessible can be used by non-state actors to expand their operations. and we see that their operations are becoming ever more sophisticated. This brings into the whole situation a new element to the challenges already facing international shipping. The convergence between emerging technologies, the proliferation of weapons that feed conflicts, and the involvement of non-state actors requires renewed attention by this Council and the international community. Given this reality, Panama feels that we need to move from a reactive posture to a preventive and coordinated approach. We must strengthen our collective capacity to anticipate new forms of threats and avoid technological progress being used to undermine international law and threaten commercial shipping or to further destabilize these strategically important shipping corridors. Panama believes it's essential to strengthen information exchange, early warning systems and cooperation between states, as well as the capacity to protect merchant vessels. seafarers and critical maritime infrastructure. Chair, the security of maritime routes is not just an issue of trade. It's also an issue of international security, energy security, and the well-being of millions of people throughout the world who depend on safe and predictable supply chains. An effective response requires coordination, prevention, and collective responsibility. Thank you very much, Chair.
I thank the distinguished representative of Panama for the statement. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Greece. You have the floor.

Your Excellency. I thank Bahrain for convening this important meeting on an issue of critical importance to international peace and security, and I welcome the presence of His Excellency, the Minister of Foreign Affairs of the Kingdom of Bahrain, in today's meeting. For Greece, maritime security remains a strategic topic of fundamental and enduring importance. And I would like to thank the briefers for their insightful contributions, which helped shed light to the importance of our topic. In recent months, the international community is witnessing an escalation in attacks against international shipping, both in frequency and intensity, by state and non-state actors. These threats are expanding in scope and nature, including through the growing use of emerging technologies and the proliferation of advanced weaponry, such as ballistic missiles and UAVs. The radically deteriorating security environment across the Strait of Hormuz, the Red Sea, the Gulf of Aden, and the Bab al-Mandeb Strait underscores a direct threat to the civilian populations, jeopardizing safety, livelihoods, and freedom of movement. The human cost of this escalation, therefore, needs to remain at the center of our response. I will make four points. First, freedom of navigation and the right to safe, open, and unimpeded passage are fundamental, non-negotiable principles. The international law of the sea is essential to the maintenance of international peace and security and global trade. We do not lack established rules. What is required of us is the full, consistent and effective implementation of the rules that already exist. They cannot be selectively applied, circumvented, or subject to conditionality upon unilateral demands or arbitrary restrictions, including unjustified tolls or other financial exactions. The existing international legal framework with the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea at its core provides the essential legal foundation for the security and stability of the maritime domain. UNCLOS sets out the universal and unified legal framework within which all activities in the oceans and seas must be carried out. Second, Equal attention should be given to the maritime governance architecture and the institutions that underpin it. Addressing today's complex maritime security challenges calls for a coordinated, multi-pronged response. The International Maritime Organization is central to this architecture. At the same time, maritime security spans multiple institutional mandates. This calls for closer coordination and complementarity among the mandates, capabilities, and efforts of relevant UN entities, international and regional organizations. The Security Council has its own part to play here, particularly where threats to maritime security bear directly on international peace and security. Dedicated and regular discussions on maritime security are important to coherently address threats, strengthen coordination, and reinforce the implementation of existing obligations and relevant United Nations Security Council resolutions. Third, we must engage substantively with and listen closely to the private sector, including shipping companies, ship owners, operators, port authorities, insurers, seafarers, and seafarers' unions. Seafarers, in particular, must be at the heart of this work. They are directly exposed to attacks and disruptions to maritime navigation. Their safety, security and welfare should be woven into international efforts to strengthen maritime security. Finally, effective maritime security depends on closer operational cooperation and complementarity among existing mechanisms and actions. We should strengthen maritime domain awareness through timely information and intelligence sharing among flag states, coastal states, the private sector, and relevant international and regional organization. Mr. President, Greece, a leading maritime nation whose history, economy, and identity are closely linked with the seas, has an abiding stake in the respect of the freedom of navigation and the safe and unimpeded passage of commercial vessels. We remain committed to keeping this vital issue on the Council's agenda. I thank you.
I thank the representative of Greece for her statement and give the floor to the representative of the United States.

Also, thank you to the briefers for their perspectives on the challenges facing the maritime domain. Freedom of navigation is not an abstract principle. It is the lifeblood of the global economy. Disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz, Bab el-Mandeb, the Gulf of Oman, and the Red Sea have shown how quickly instability at a single choke point can affect global energy, food, and humanitarian supply chains. In the face of these threats, President Trump directed firm action to safeguard maritime security and protect seafarers and commercial shipping. The Iranian regime and its partners and proxies, including the Houthis, remain the principal source of this insecurity. Security Council Resolution 2817 adopted with 136 co-sponsors, clearly showed the international community's overwhelming demand that Iran and its partners cease attacks on shipping and neighboring states. Iran repeatedly defies that resolution, firing missiles and drones at commercial vessels and attacking its neighbors, Bahrain, Jordan, Kuwait, Oman, Qatar, and the UAE. The Houthis, emboldened by Iranian support, terrorize maritime traffic in the Red Sea and the Gulf of Aden for years, affecting nearly 30% of international container traffic. Recently, the Houthis attacked Saudi commercial vessels while enforcing a self-declared embargo to dictate maritime traffic around Bab al-Mandeb. These actions are in defiance of Security Council Resolutions 2216 and 2817 and will not be tolerated. The United States will not stand by while Iran and its partners and proxies attempt to hold hostage the global economy. As President Trump made clear, the clock is ticking for Iran to end its attacks, remove its mines from the Strait of Hormuz, and allow for the free passage of commercial shipping and humanitarian goods. Peace through strength remains our guiding principle. Deterrence, backed by credible capability, preserves open sea lanes and protects innocent mariners. We urge all council members, including those who shield Iran from consequences, to stand firmly for the rule of international law and the safety of commercial shipping. The United States stands ready to work with Bahrain, our Gulf partners, and this Council to build mechanisms for maritime security that protect seafarers, safeguard trade, and preserve peace.

Thank you.
I thank the representative of the United States for her statement and give the floor to the representative of Somalia.

Good afternoon, Mr. Chair. Somalia thanks the Kingdom of Bahrain for convening this timely Arria formula meeting. I warmly welcome His Excellency, the Prime Minister of Foreign Affairs of the Kingdom of Bahrain, who is chairing today's meeting, and thank you to our distinguished briefers for their valuable contributions. We welcome the opportunity to address maritime security, which is directly linked to international peace and security, global trade, economic stability, humanitarian access, and seafarer safety. For Somalia, With the longest coastline on mainland Africa and situated at the crossroads of the Indian Ocean, Gulf of Aden, and the Red Sea, the security and sustainable management of our maritime domain are matters of national and regional importance. Recent disruptions in maritime navigation demonstrate how threats in one maritime area can affect energy flows, food security, global supply chains, and humanitarian operations. They also show how disruption at one maritime route can trigger cascading consequences across interconnected waterways and the global trading system. In this vein, Somalia wishes to emphasize the following points. First, international law must remain the foundation of maritime security. UNCLOS and other relevant instruments provide the legal framework for activities at sea, including navigation through straits used for international navigation. freedom of navigation, and the right to transit passage must be respected, with due regard for the sovereignty, territorial integrity, and legitimate security interests of coastal states. As reaffirmed by Security Council Resolution 2817, transit passage must not be unlawfully impeded. Navigational rights must be upheld to ensure safe, secure, and commercially viable passage. Second, Maritime security requires a comprehensive approach. Military measures alone are insufficient. We need stronger maritime domain awareness, information sharing, early warning, and crisis communication, as well as contingency planning for simultaneous or cascading disruptions. We must prepare for overlapping crises. Contingency planning should consider simultaneous disruptions across interconnected waterways and their effects on ports, fuel supplies, insurance, food supply chains, and humanitarian deliveries, particularly where alternative routes are limited. Our institutions must keep pace with evolving risks, including unmanned systems and cyber attacks. Such support should be predictable, coordinated, and guided by national priorities. Third, national ownership and regional cooperation are essential. Coastal states require sustained support for coast guards, surveillance, search and rescue, support security, law enforcement, and judicial institutions. The United Nations, IMO, member states, regional organizations, and the maritime industry should strengthen standing or rapidly deployable incident response arrangements. We must also address the economic and environmental consequences of insecurity, particularly for developing countries. Regional cooperation must also address illegal, unreported, or unregulated fishing, trafficking, or smuggling. African Union frameworks and the UNDE architecture should be strengthened rather than duplicated, with relevant private sector actors fully engaged. In conclusion, Somalia is mindful of our shared responsibility for the security and stability of our oceans and seas. Addressing these challenges requires a unified collective approach. grounded in international cooperation and the rule of law. My delegation reaffirms its commitment to working constructively with the Security Council and the broader international community to realize the vision of safe, secure, and prosperous seas for all, ensuring our waterways remain a bridge of peace and prosperity, connecting nations rather than dividing them. Thank you, Mr. President.
I thank the representative of Somalia for her statement and give the floor to the representative of Russia.

Mr. Chairman, distinguished Minister Al-Zayani, we welcome your personal chairmanship of today's informal Rio Formula meeting of Security Council members, and we thank the briefers for their statements and their contribution to this discussion. the same time, we would like to, from the outset, state that issues of maritime security are not directly related to the mandate of the Security Council. We have consistently worked on the basis of the understanding that, in order to have a substantive consideration of them, there exist other specialized forums. It is regrettable that the concept note for today's meeting does not mention in any way the most serious and a truly global challenge to navigation in the world's ocean. And we refer to attempts by European Union countries and the United Kingdom, relying on the unilateral coercive measures illegally imposed by themselves in violation of international law to seize civilian vessels. Such actions constitute a gross violation of the fundamental provisions of the 1982 United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea, which guarantees freedom of navigation and the right of peaceful and transit passage. They undermine the very foundation of the stability and predictability of supply chains and, as a consequence, create a serious threat to global trade, a significant part of which is carried out by sea. The stability and predictability of maritime logistics are important for all countries, and for small island states or coastal developing states, this is in actual fact a matter of survival. The imposition by the collective West of illegal unilateral coercive measures in addition to affecting the countries against which they are directed, also impacts an unlimited number of third states for which the consequences of it may range from higher prices of certain types of goods to disruptions in the supply of critically important goods, including such things as food and hydrocarbons. Both the unilateral coercive measures that contravene international law and the restrictions on freedom of navigation, which are their unlawful consequence, accompanied by attaching to vessels the label of belonging to so-called shadow fleet, pursue one and the same objective in securing their own dominance through unfair competition by non-economic means. Right before our eyes, a narrow group of countries consisting almost entirely of former colonial powers is attempting to reserve for itself a monopoly position in the maritime transport market. And we think it's unnecessary to explain what such a situation means for states significantly or entirely dependent on maritime transport. We would like also to separately emphasize that neither international law nor the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea does the concept of a shadow fleet exist. Neither any mention of it nor any reference to unilateral coercive measures can be found in the strictly limited list of grounds for stopping and inspecting vessels at sea. Therefore, the actions of the European pirates of the 21st century have no legal basis whatsoever, Mr. Chair. As concerns the situation in the Strait of Hormuz and the Bab al-Mandeb Strait, as well as in the Gulf of Oman and in the Red Sea, we are convinced that this issue cannot be considered in isolation from the broader regional context. The escalation observed there is a direct consequence of the reckless American-Israeli military adventure. And it was precisely the unprovoked aggression against Iran that set an entire region ablaze. The focus by some delegations on Tehran's responsive actions is an obvious substitution of cause and effect. And this point is best illustrated by the simple fact that before the 28th of February 2026, no disruptions in the movement of commercial vessels in the Persian Gulf area had been observed. We are convinced that the only way to resolve problems with navigations in the above-mentioned waterways is through political and diplomatic efforts aimed at a sustainable settlement of the conflict while taking into account the legitimate rights and interests of all regional states. We expect that the parties will return to the negotiating table as soon as possible, and we are grateful to the States providing them with assistance in this work. For our part, we also stand ready to provide all the necessary support. I thank you for your attention.
I thank the representative of Russia for her statement and give the floor to Colombia. The floor is yours.

Thank you, Chair. Allow me to congratulate the Kingdom of Bahrain for convening this very valuable debate on a subject of concern to all of us. And I'd like to welcome the Minister of Foreign Affairs of Bahrain leading our discussions today. Colombia would like to begin by expressing our deep concern at the developments in the Middle East. This is clearly not a de-escalation, it's an escalation of the conflict with the corresponding loss of human lives and with ongoing disruption to the freedom of navigation and its harmful effects for international peace and security. Colombia also recognizes the strategic importance of the straits for international commerce, energy security, and food security. Anything that disrupts safe shipping has impacts beyond the region where this is happening, and it particularly disproportionately affects developing countries. Chair, Colombia is a maritime nation with coasts on both oceans, and we're very much concerned about the sustainable use of natural resources. Due to our geostrategic location, Colombia is exposed to very many maritime security challenges, including maritime drug trafficking, illegal fishing, irregular migration, arms and fuel contraband, and we need to protect our marine natural environments as well. Colombia is not a party to UNCLOS, but we do recognize that it does regulate very much of the maritime area, particularly with regard to the freedom of navigation. And unfortunately, UNCLOS doesn't provide us with all of the answers to all of the circumstances that pertain to the freedom of navigation. Among those reasons is that UNCLOS is designed to be applied in times of peace, and when conflict arises, UNCLOS cannot provide all the answers. Given that regulatory vacuum, when there are violations of existing laws, it is the Security Council that must fulfil the role for which it was established. the Council is able to send out clear messages aimed at containing and preventing greater escalation and ensure respect for the United Nations Charter and international law. Having said that, the role of the Council is only a part of the problem, which has many aspects to it. Maritime security must be addressed from the approach of cooperation between naval forces, civilian agencies, regional organizations, multilateral partners, and the private sector. One country cannot deal with this alone, or one agency or one organization cannot deal with it alone, given the multiple threats that freedom of shipping is facing. Colombia welcomes any initiatives aimed at strengthening international cooperation to address maritime challenges, including to strengthen respect for the law of the sea and increase the abilities of developing countries and regional organizations to act in areas such as Latin America and the Caribbean. Second, on credible reporting and accountability, we believe that relevant actors should preserve evidence and share verified information appropriately.

Investigations must be partial and evidence-based. with attribution supported where needed for forensic, legal, and technical assistance. Third, on capacity and resilience, developing coastal states need predictable support to monitor their waters, protect ports and maritime infrastructure, strengthen cyber resilience, and respond to emergencies. Assistance must reflect national priorities and include training, maintenance, and sustained operational resources. Excellencies, the seas connect our economies and our futures. We encourage the Chair to reflect these priorities in its summary and support practical follow-up that protects seafarers and keeps maritime routes safe, open, and resilient.

Thank you.
I thank the Permanent Representative of Timor-Leste for this statement, and I'll give the floor to the Permanent Representative of Germany.

Thank you, President. Thank you to the briefers for the valuable input, and thank you for convening this meeting today, because indeed, our maritime security requires a collective attention. Freedom of the seas is a lifeline of our interconnected global economy. Others have said so, but I would like to underline as well. Maritime disruptions have devastating consequences on trade, food and energy security and stability that reach far beyond the region. And the conflicts in the Strait of Hormuz, the Red Sea and around the Black Sea are testimony to that, and they underline that the law of the sea needs to be upheld. Maritime security must be based on international law and on the principles of navigational rights and freedom. By threatening and attacking international commercial shipping, Iran is violating international law. Just as the Houthis are doing in the Bab al-Mandab. And with its shadow fleet, Russia continues to misuse the right of peaceful transit, to attack sea cables, to engage in espionage, and it risks massive accidents and environmental damage. So what are we to do in light of these conflicts? A few points. One, the United Nations Convention of the Law of the Sea provides the international legal framework for all activities in the oceans and seas, and we need to uphold it and strengthen it. Secondly, we need to restore and preserve navigational rights and freedom in the Strait of Hormuz, the Bab al-Mandab, and elsewhere. Thirdly, we need both effective protection for ships and seafarers, and we need accountability for attacks when they happen and for unlawful interference with commercial shipping in order to prevent choke points being used as leverage against our economies. And fourth, these conflicts also remind us to strengthen early warning and coordination among states, the UN, regional organizations, and maritime industry. And I think all of us can do things concretely, and we need to think about what we can do. Just by ways of example, Germany is fully committed by, for example, supporting the EU naval force mission, ESDAS. where we contribute to the protection of international shipping in the Red Sea and adjacent waters, through support of IRINI and UNIFIL. We support maritime security in the Mediterranean, in line with UN Security Council resolutions. And we support the EU's initiative on the protection of critical maritime infrastructure that has been launched by High Representative Kallas at the EU Indo-Pacific Ministerial Forum last year. We support a number of further regional initiatives, particularly through the G7+ Friends of the Gulf of Guinea platform and in cooperation with IMO and UNITAR. Just to mention this, that there are ways to secure our waterways, to strengthen maritime security if we act collectively, and I want to ensure you that Germany will remain a steady contributor substantially and concretely to maritime security. Thank you very much.

I thank the distinguished permanent representative of Germany. I now give the floor to the distinguished permanent representative of Japan, followed by the permanent representative of India, then Bulgaria, then Argentina. Japan.

Thank you, Chair. India thanks the Kingdom of Bahrain for convening this Area Formula meeting. We also thank the briefers for their remarks on this important issue. India is a major maritime nation, and we strongly support a free, open, secure, and rules-based maritime domain. Rights and freedoms of navigation and overflight should be consistent with international law, including United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea, which must be fully respected. Commercial vessels must not become targets of geopolitical tensions. Navigational rights must not be subjected to coercion, threats, unlawful restrictions, or arbitrary interference. Equally vital are coordinated evacuation frameworks for seafarers. in conflict zones with clear responsibilities among states and international organizations. India has been contributing in a sustained manner for maritime security in the Indo-Pacific region. As on 14th September of this year, continued maritime security operations in the Gulf of Aden and the Red Sea have ensured safe transit to more than 449 merchant vessels, carrying nearly 20.3 million metric tons of cargo and oil worth more than $8.4 billion. Their safety, timely evacuation, medical assistance, crew changes, and repatriation require effective contingency planning and international cooperation. Their safety and security require much greater attention in the present circumstances. Countries with considerable interest in terms of safety and security of shipping and seafarers must come together. International cooperation, capacity building, and responsible use of technology will be critical in addressing these challenges. Chair, the objective should not merely be to restore navigation after a crisis, but to build a maritime system capable of withstanding shocks before they cascade into wider economic and humanitarian crisis. India stands ready to work constructively with member states to strengthen maritime security, protect seafarers, uphold navigational freedoms, and ensure resilient and uninterrupted international commerce. Thank you, Chair.

Mr. Ambassador, Mr. Foreign Affairs, I'd like to thank Bahrain for this initiative, giving us the chance to reflect again on something that affects us all, namely the security of maritime corridors. the ocean brings together much more than it separates. The United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea is the fundamental legal framework within which all activities on the oceans and seas must be carried out. Within that framework, we should remember that blocking maritime traffic through an international strait by a coastal state constitutes a violation of international law. In accordance with UNCLOS, the right of transit and passage must be guaranteed and never hindered. This conviction led us to co-sponsor the Security Council resolution condemning Iran for its actions threatening international trade and passage through the Strait of Hormuz. Maritime security also has a very human dimension to it. Behind every vessel, there is a team. Behind every cargo, there's a supply chain. And behind every delay, there could be fuel, food, or goods that are essential and waiting to arrive at their destination. Protecting shipping is also protecting life, economies, and the marine environment. The current challenges also present new dimensions, namely the use of unmanned aerial vehicles and interference with navigation and communication systems can all increase risks for commercial shipping and for the security of seafarers. As part of this effort, the IMO has a central role to play in the exchange of information, leading to giving us greater awareness of what's happening in the marine environment and the importance for the responsible use of new technologies. Thank you.
I thank the Permanent Representative of Argentina. I now give the floor to the Permanent Representative of Albania.

Thank you. Thank you, Mr. President. We thank the Kingdom of Bahrain for convening this meeting. And of course, we align ourselves to the statement to be delivered by the European Union. And we had some further remarks in national capacity. Maritime threats pose significant challenges, not just to coastal states and local communities, but also to the international community as a whole. The breadth of these threats, especially those affecting critical maritime routes, is growing so much that it has become one of the main drivers of global instability. The increasing disruptions to commercial shipping, notably in the Gulf, the Strait of Hormuz, Bab el-Mandeb, the Gulf of Oman, and the Red Sea, in blatant violation of international law, are a stark reminder of the fundamental importance of maritime communication routes for the international economy and, ultimately, for international peace and security. Accordingly, it is in the interest of every state to commit to ensuring the full application of the principle of freedom of navigation and under safe conditions for maritime personnel. Mr. President, Italy reiterates its solidarity towards the Gulf countries affected by unacceptable retaliatory strikes. In particular, while condemning in the strongest possible terms the recent Houthi attacks against Saudi Arabia and against the legitimate Yemeni government, Italy expresses the urgency of putting an end to hostilities and to preserve the freedom and safety of navigation in the Red Sea and through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait. Italy, including through EU NAVFOR ASPIDES, will continue to do its part to safeguard freedom of navigation and contribute to maritime safety and the stability of the region. At the same time, Italy stresses once again the need for collective action to ensure universal compliance with the relevant international norms. UNCLOS remains the fundamental legal framework for maritime rights and obligations, including those related to maritime security. In the same vein, we are affirming the Security Council's primary responsibility in addressing challenges to maritime security capable of disrupting global navigation and trade, damaging critical infrastructures and destabilizing regional stability. Building on the legal foundation provided by the Charter of the United Nations, UNCLOS and other key conventions, the Security Council can promote the adoption of legal norms and resolutions, address regional crises involving critical sea passages and choke points, authorize actions against maritime threats such as piracy, terrorism and various illicit activities. While the Security Council can offer guidance to resolve any disputes or disagreements with regard to maritime security and address threats to the freedom of navigation, its effective implementation rests on Member States' willingness and commitment. Italy has been supporting international efforts against any threat to maritime security and stands ready to contribute to collective efforts, concerted with regional and international partners and defensive in nature, to safeguard the freedom of navigation and to preserve the stability of the global markets in the Gulf, the Straits of Hormuz, the Red Sea and elsewhere. We will remain steadfast in our commitment to upholding freedom of navigation globally and reinforcing the law of the sea. I thank you.

The distinguished representative of Italy, and I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of the European Union.

Thank you, Mr. President. I have the honor to speak on behalf of the European Union and its member states. The candidate countries North Macedonia, Montenegro, Albania, Ukraine, the Republic of Moldova, and Bosnia and Herzegovina, as well as Monaco, align themselves with this statement. Let me begin by thanking you, Mr. President, and the Kingdom of Bahrain for convening this meeting, and of course the briefers for their contributions. As President von der Leyen underlined in yesterday's State of the Union address, disruption in the Strait of Hormuz has had direct consequences for Europe's energy security and economy. with imported fossil fuels costing Europe an additional 90 billion since the start of the conflict. This was a stark reminder, if any were needed, that disruption to the strategic maritime routes has consequences far beyond the region. The EU recalls the universal and unified character of the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea, as many others have in this room, which sets out the legal framework within which all activities in the oceans and seas must be carried out. We reiterate the need to maintain the integrity of the Convention. Preserving a stable and open international maritime order based on the rule of law and international law is both a legal obligation and a shared global interest. In this context, on the Strait of Hormuz, the EU and the Gulf Cooperation Council reaffirmed together in Brussels on 13 July that freedom of navigation, including the right of passage through the Strait, is guaranteed under international law as reflected in UNCLOS. These rights belong to the ships of all states and cannot be suspended, impeded, or made conditional by any state. Passage cannot be subject to permits, transit tolls, or general service fees, discrimination, or unlawful authorization requirements. Introducing restrictions, conditions, discriminatory measures, or other obstacles to lawful passage through international straits would be patently illegal and set a dangerous precedent for global strategic waterways. The European Council has called for the full implementation of UNSC Resolution 2817 and condemned any acts that threaten navigation or prevent vessels from entering and exiting the Strait. President, the EU is also seriously concerned by the dangerous escalation around Bab el-Mandeb. Houthi attacks and threats against Saudi Arabia and Saudi-linked vessels have reduced the overall number of ships transiting the Bab el-Mandeb Strait. We recall UN Security Council Resolution 2722, which demands that the Houthis immediately cease all attacks on merchant and commercial vessels. President, another major choke point for freedom of navigation is the Black Sea. Russia has intensified attacks against ports and commercial shipping. including drone and missile attacks against oil tankers, resulting in multiple deaths of seafarers, together with systematic strikes against inland logistics, warehouses, and grain terminals, in violation of international law, including UNCLOS. This recent escalation is severely disrupting freedom of navigation, global energy, and food supply chains, risking global hunger. This is unacceptable. Chair, The EU will continue to work within and support international and regional institutions responsible for maritime governance, safety and security, particularly the International Maritime Organization. The EU also supports and promotes regional cooperation for maritime security. Finally, President, diplomacy remains essential to resolving outstanding issues, so in closing, We wish to commend regional partners for the mediation efforts. The full statement will be published online. Thank you, Mr. President. I.
Thank the distinguished representative of the European Union, and I'll give the floor to the distinguished representative of the Netherlands.

Thank you, Mr. President, and I must start by showing my appreciation for allowing us to speak at this hour of the day. These are long days. The Kingdom of the Netherlands aligns itself with the statement just made by my colleague of the European Union. The freedom of navigation has been key policy priority for the Kingdom of the Netherlands for over four centuries. Freedom of navigation is a fundamental principle of international law, including under the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea, UNCLOS. Working together to maintain free and safe seas has become increasingly crucial in our modern, globalised world. In this regard, I would like to make three points. Firstly, on the Strait of Hormuz. The Kingdom of the Netherlands condemns in the strongest terms the inexcusable attacks by Iran on unarmed commercial vessels in the Gulf, and the de facto closure of the Strait of Hormuz by Iranian forces. We call on Iran to immediately cease its threats, laying of mines, drone and missile attacks, and other attempts to obstruct commercial shipping through the Strait. We call upon Iran to comply with Resolution 2817 and to respect the sovereign territorial waters of other littoral states, including those of the Sultanate of Oman. Moreover, we reject any post-conflict arrangements which include tolls or other restrictive mechanisms not in full accordance with international law as reflected in UNCLOS. Any potential post-conflict mechanism of internationalisation should be cognisant of the legitimate interests of all littoral states. Secondly, on the Red Sea, the Kingdom of the Netherlands strongly condemns similar attempts of the Houthis to obstruct shipping lanes in the Red Sea and Bab al-Mandab through drone and missile attacks on commercial vessels. Thirdly, on the need for diplomacy, the Kingdom of the Netherlands commends all those who are working tirelessly towards a diplomatic solution to restore the freedom of navigation. In particular, we welcome the efforts of the Sultanate of Oman and the State of Qatar. In conclusion, the urgent reopening of the Strait of Hormuz with unconditional and unrestricted freedom of navigation is essential. The Kingdom of the Netherlands continues to believe in a diplomatic solution and is committed to play its part in achieving this. This includes our intention to participate in the multinational military mission for the Strait of Hormuz, a defensive military mission to reassure commercial shipping and conduct mine clearance operations once the situation allows it. I thank you very much.

I thank the distinguished representative of the Netherlands for her statement. We have thus heard the last speaker in our session today. And I would like to express my sincere apologies to those delegations that we were unable to listen to because of the time constraints, I do hope that delegations that were unable to take the floor, we hope that they could send us their texts so that we could include them in the President's summary of this meeting, this important meeting, and allow me to make a few concluding observations on our meeting today. Our discussions today have reaffirmed that the security of vital waterways is a joint responsibility. The threats that are posed to the Strait of Hormuz, Bab el-Mandeb, the Gulf of Oman, and the Red Sea have repercussions that go far beyond the vessels and the areas that are directly affected. Their repercussions extend to the international energy markets and international food supply chains, as well as humanitarian aid and the global economy as a whole.
